memory.how: From `/usr/bin/time -l` on each server when it stopped, in the second of two runs (Apple M5, 16 GB, `--ctx-size 8192`). Model files are memory-mapped, so these numbers move with memory pressure: in the first run the 4B server showed 1,873 MB resident and 1,436 MB footprint, and alone it showed 3,337 MB and 1,266 MB. The three files total 8.7 GB, so treat that as the real need. All three ran together, and free memory reported by `memory_pressure` fell to 14% at its lowest reading.

bugs.title: A crash just before the reply reported the booking twice
bugs.what_broke: `test_crash_before_reply` (scenario 37) failed with `assert 2 == 1`. After a restart, the user saw "Booked and verified" twice.
bugs.why: the outcome is saved in the same transaction as `DONE`, so a crash can never lose it. The turn's final reply then repeats that text and is saved as a second undelivered row. A crash between saving the reply and returning it left both rows undelivered.
bugs.fix: saving the final reply now marks the outcome rows it replaces as delivered, in one transaction, so exactly one of them can ever be shown again (`src/errand/runner.py`).

bugs.title: Reaching any cap crashed the handler that should tell the user
bugs.what_broke: `test_model_call_cap`, `test_tool_call_cap` and `test_wall_clock_cap` failed with `TypeError: Tracer.event() got multiple values for argument 'kind'`. The cap was enforced, but the turn then died with no message to the user, which is exactly what must-have 5 forbids.
bugs.why: the first parameter of `Tracer.event` was named `kind`, and the cap handler passed a trace field also called `kind`. The failure only appears on a path that normal bookings never take.
bugs.fix: the event type is now a positional-only parameter, so no trace field name can clash with it (`src/errand/infra/trace.py`).

bugs.title: The model call that created a run did not count against that run
bugs.what_broke: `test_per_run_cap_with_proposal_pending` (scenario 35) failed: with `run_model_calls=1`, the run stayed in `AWAITING_APPROVAL` when it should have moved to `FAILED`. The per-run cap allowed one more model call than configured.
bugs.why: a run is created by the model's own `set_intent` action, so that call was charged to the turn while no run was attached yet. The run's counter started at zero.
bugs.fix: a new run starts with the calls its creating turn has already made (`_set_intent` in `src/errand/core/workflow.py`).

bugs.title: A retry blocked by a cap was still counted, which made a promise to the user false
bugs.what_broke: `test_cap_with_write_in_flight` (scenario 31) failed with `assert 0 == 1` in the ledger. The agent told the user "I will try again when you next reply", then on the next message said it had run out of retries, with no further `book` call.
bugs.why: a retry was counted when it was scheduled, not when it was sent. The cap then stopped that call, so a retry was used up with nothing sent.
bugs.fix: when a cap stops a call in `EXECUTING`, the retry counted for it is given back (`verify_after_cap` in `src/errand/core/workflow.py`).

bugs.title: "Stop" during a re-hold could still book
bugs.what_broke: `test_stop_during_a_rehold_never_books` failed: the ledger held a booking after the user said stop. A code review found this path by hand-tracing, and the test reproduced it before the fix.
bugs.why: after `hold_expired`, the run sits in `HOLDING` with an approved attempt. The stop logic only ran on the way through `VERIFYING`, so a stop in `HOLDING` carried on to a new hold and then `book`, and the user was told it was "already booked when you asked to stop".
bugs.fix: a re-hold now checks for a stop or a forgotten value first, and ends the run with no write (`_abort_rehold` in `src/errand/core/workflow.py`).

bugs.title: The output schema forced the live model to invent a provider preference
bugs.what_broke: the first run against the real model turned "Find a plumber for my kitchen tap this week, mornings only, under ₹1,500" into `{"service":"plumber","when":"this_week","latest_time":"12:00","provider":"same_as_last"}`. The budget was gone, and a preference the user never stated had appeared. The output was valid, so nothing rejected it. Every scripted test passed, because scripted models skip the grammar.
bugs.why: llama.cpp's grammar fixes the order of an object's keys. Once the model had written `latest_time` and a comma, `provider` was the only legal next key, and `budget` could no longer be written at all.
bugs.fix: each detail is now its own action. A list can take details in any order and can end at any point, so no key is ever forced (`output_schema` in `src/errand/interpret/llama.py`).

bugs.title: The live model repeated itself until a cap stopped it
bugs.what_broke: asking about reviews printed the same provider five times and ended with "I reached my limit on thinking steps". Then "the cheapest one" replied "Sorry, I did not understand that" just above the correct proposal. The trace showed `request_read` five times, and `select_option` three times with two rejected in `HOLDING`.
bugs.why: the model could return `done: false`, which asks for another step on the same message. Nothing new reaches it on that step, so at temperature 0 it returned the same action again. Scripted models returned exactly what each test wanted, so this never appeared.
bugs.fix: the live schema fixes `done` to true, so the grammar cannot express a second step. The caps still stop any other model that loops.

bugs.title: "yes?" approved a booking
bugs.what_broke: `test_a_question_is_not_an_approval` failed: with a proposal showing, "book it?", "ok?" and "yes?" each counted as approval. A fresh review spotted it, and the test reproduced it. This breaks must-have 2 directly, in the rule that "yes, but" was built to protect.
bugs.why: intake removed all trailing punctuation before matching the list of bare confirmations, including the question mark that shows the user is asking, not agreeing.
bugs.fix: intake no longer removes a question mark before matching confirmations (`_normalise` in `src/errand/core/intake.py`).

bugs.title: A stop was forgotten after one turn, and the next message booked anyway
bugs.what_broke: `test_a_stop_given_while_the_outcome_is_unknown_still_applies_on_the_next_message` failed. `book` timed out and status gave no answer. The user said stop and was told "your stop takes effect once it is known". Their next message made a second `book` call and replied "Booked and verified". A restart did the same.
bugs.why: the stop was held on the `Turn` object, which lasts one message, so the promise made to the user could not survive to the moment it had to be kept.
bugs.fix: the stop is saved on the run (`stop_requested` in `src/errand/core/domain.py`).

bugs.title: "book it" approved a cancel
bugs.what_broke: `test_words_naming_booking_cannot_approve_a_cancel` failed: with a cancel proposal showing, "book it" replied "Cancelled and verified". A fresh review found it while checking new Hindi words such as "book kar do", which widened an existing gap.
bugs.why: intake reduced every confirmation to a plain yes, so the action the user named was lost before it could be compared with the action on the proposal.
bugs.fix: a confirmation that names an action keeps that name, and it cannot confirm a different action (`names_action` in `src/errand/core/intake.py`, checked in `_answer_approval` in `src/errand/core/workflow.py`).

bugs.title: A tab left open approved a proposal it had never shown
bugs.what_broke: `test_a_stale_tab_cannot_approve_a_proposal_in_a_newer_session` failed. A fresh review reproduced it in Chrome: tab A showed a booking at 08:00, tab B started a new session and showed 09:00, and tab A's "yes" booked 09:00, with no stale event.
bugs.why: the stale check compares reply ids, and reply ids restart in each session. Both proposals had id 2, so the engine could not tell the two tabs apart.
bugs.fix: each message names the session its page is showing, checked on the engine's thread, so a message for an older session is refused (`Sessions.say` in `src/errand/web/chat.py`).
